text:
Navigating the AI Vocabulary
In practice, researchers encounter a scattered soup of overlapping terms and tools:


Linear & Logistic Regression ChatGPT / Claude / Perplexity Symbolic Logic & Rules PCA / UMAP CNN & RNN Data Science & Statistics Random Forest & Decision Trees Intelligent Robots Neural Networks (MLP) Support Vector Machines (SVM) Knowledge Representation


Which field contains which—and where do everyday chatbots actually sit?



Spoken core (20 sec): When you start reading AI literature as a domain researcher, you run straight into this wall of overlapping terms—regressions, PCA, random forests, CNNs, symbolic rules, and chatbots all thrown into the same conversation.
Callback: Connects the four messy Venn diagrams on Slide 8 to the concrete tools researchers encounter.
Bridge: Let’s sort these pills into their actual nested structure.

title: AI for Ecotoxicologists
text:
Navigating the AI Vocabulary
Organizing the umbrella into parallel domains and nested subsets:

ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE (Umbrella Discipline)



Symbolic AI, Reasoning & Embodied Systems

Symbolic Logic & Rules Knowledge Representation Intelligent Robots


Explicit rules, ontologies, and constraint solving (e.g., protected-area design in CESAB Day 5).


Overlapping Quantitative Pillar Data Science & Statistics





MACHINE LEARNING (Automated Learning from Data)

Linear & Logistic Regression PCA / UMAP Support Vector Machines (SVM) Random Forest & Decision Trees


DEEP LEARNING (Multi-Layer Neural Networks)

Neural Networks (MLP) CNN & RNN


GENERATIVE AI & LLMs (A small, highly visible subset) ChatGPT / Claude / Perplexity







Standard reference taxonomy: The OECD Framework for the Classification of AI Systems classifies systems by model type (symbolic, statistical, or hybrid), learning paradigm, and transparency.



Spoken core: Point directly to the small red box at the bottom right (GenAI / LLMs). Reconnect explicitly to Slide 2’s word cloud: GenAI dominates our mental picture not because it is all of AI, but because of accessibility—anyone can ask a chatbot for a dinner recipe, whereas very few people will train a CNN or build a constraint solver. Be candid: AI capabilities are advancing rapidly and producing real scientific breakthroughs (like AlphaFold), so denying its utility makes no sense.
Callback: Closes the loop on Slide 2’s word cloud bias and sets up the taxonomy needed to understand where neural networks and LLMs live.
Bridge: And this leads directly to a personal misconception—and a paradox—that hit close to home for me when I began learning these methods…

title: AI for Ecotoxicologists
section: A Personal Misconception & The Bio-Inspired Paradox
text:
A Personal Misconception & The Bio-Inspired Paradox
When I started learning ML, I assumed neural networks worked like my brain processing thoughts.

Inspired by biology — not biologically grounded (like a movie “based on true events”)





Biological Brain

~20 W power budget; slow electrochemical ionic spikes.
Diverse chemical neurotransmitters & local synaptic plasticity.
Learns flexibly and generalizes from few exposures.



[IMAGE: Biological Brain / Synaptic Network] Save file as: assets/images/bio_brain_network.png 






Artificial Neural Networks

Matrix multiplications over floating-point weights.
Global backpropagation optimizing a mathematical loss function.
Requires massive datasets and computational energy.



[IMAGE: Artificial Neural Network / Perceptron Layers] Save file as: assets/images/ann_perceptron_layers.png 





The Paradox: Tools loosely inspired by human cognition are increasingly used in ways that short-circuit the very biological process our brains need to learn.


Conceptual inspiration: A. Andalman (The Deep View, 2025) · C. Simon (AI Neuro Insight, 2025) · A. Karpathy (Dwarkesh Clips, 2025) · AlphaFold (Nobel Prize in Chemistry, 2024)



Spoken core: Use my own initial misconception as a teaching moment: coming from biology, I first imagined artificial neurons as miniature reasoning units. In reality, biological brains run on ~20 watts with slow chemical signaling and local learning rules, whereas ANNs do fast matrix algebra and global backpropagation—they share inspiration, not mechanism. Click to reveal the paradox: these bio-inspired tools are now routinely used in ways that bypass our own biological learning.
Callback: Connects directly to the Deep Learning & GenAI nested boxes we just mapped on Slide 10.
Bridge: Let’s look closely at how that cognitive shortcut works in everyday research practice.

title: AI for Ecotoxicologists
text:
Insight 1b: Cognitive Bypassing & Expertise Asymmetry


      Raw Information Papers · Data · Code   Effortful Processing Cognitive Friction & Schema Building   Durable Expertise & Critical Audit Capacity


       GenAI Shortcut — Bypasses Effortful Processing  Illusion of Learning & Cognitive Debt





How LLMs Actually Operate

LLMs are probabilistic next-token generators optimized for fluency—not truth-verification engines.
Externalizing core analysis risks cognitive proletarianization (Stiegler, 2010): fluent outputs can mask weak epistemic grounding and reduce retention, critical thinking, and neural engagement.





High Domain Background (Your Field): You form concrete hypotheses \(\rightarrow\) write precise prompts \(\rightarrow\) audit and catch errors.


Low Domain Background (Unfamiliar Field): Unclear what to ask \(\rightarrow\) vague prompts \(\rightarrow\) plausible errors go undetected.




Stiegler (2010) For a New Critique of Political Economy · Messeri & Crockett (2024) Nature 10.1038/s41586-024-07146-0 · Barcaui (2025) SSHO 10.1016/j.ssaho.2025.102287 · Gerlich (2025) Societies 10.3390/soc15010006 · Kosmyna et al. (2025) arXiv:2506.08872 (preprint) · Diagram adapted from J. Sung (2025)



Spoken core: Walk through the SVG first (Click 1 reveals the red shortcut): biological learning requires the middle step—cognitive friction—to build mental schemas and expertise. Skipping that step does not land on expertise faster; it lands on an illusion of learning and cognitive debt (supported by controlled studies: Barcaui 2025, Gerlich 2025, Kosmyna et al. 2025 arXiv preprint). Click 2 for the 30-second rhetorical thought experiment: imagine an ecotoxicologist asking an LLM about survival-model assumptions—they catch a subtle mistake instantly. Now imagine the same person asking it to write an unfamiliar microbial metagenomics or bioinformatics pipeline—it will return fluent, plausible code whose hidden flaws they cannot audit. Practical guardrail: keep cognitive friction for reasoning, writing, and analysis; delegate routine formatting or syntax lookup.
Callback: Directly operationalizes the bio-inspired paradox from Slide 11.
Bridge: Cognitive cost is only half the picture—there is also a physical cost behind every query.

title: AI for Ecotoxicologists
text:
Beyond Cognition: Material & Ecological Footprint
A brief factual check on the infrastructure behind large-scale AI workflows:



Energy & Resource Rebound

Net \(\text{CO}_2\) Rebound: Global energy–economy modelling indicates that AI-driven productivity gains can enable more \(\text{CO}_2\) emissions than they avoid (Alpine et al., 2026).
Local Water Competition: Rapid data-center expansion concentrates in regions with unresolved water-access pressures—for example, Uruguay (1.77) and Chile (3.49) data centers per 1 million inhabitants (IFC, 2026).
Takeaway for Scientists: Proportionality matters—do not deploy heavy generative or deep-learning compute where a lightweight statistical model already answers the question.








“Only a tiny proportion of water in Uruguay is used for human consumption.” — Daniel Pena, University of the Republic (Rest of World, 2026)




Alpine et al. (2026) npj Clim. Action 5, 71 10.1038/s44168-026-00411-0 · International Finance Corporation (IFC, 2026) · Rest of World (2026)



Spoken core (1 min — sober, factual tone): Keep this grounded and non-alarmist. Beyond cognition, AI has a real physical footprint: global models suggest rebound effects can raise net emissions (Alpine et al., 2026), and data-center placement increasingly intersects with local water stress, as seen in South America (Uruguay at 1.77 and Chile at 3.49 data centers per million inhabitants). As environmental scientists, proportionality is simply good practice.
Callback: Completes Insight 1 (both 1a taxonomy and 1b cognitive + material guardrails).
Bridge: Now that we know what sits under the AI umbrella—and the cognitive and material costs of using it blindly—how do we decide when a scientific problem genuinely justifies moving beyond classical statistics?

title: AI for Ecotoxicologists
section: When Does a Research Problem Need AI?
text:
When Does a Research Problem Need AI?
Scenario: Monitoring 100 river sites across temperature, water chemistry, pollutants, and species communities.



What Is a “Dimension”?

In Ecology / Env. Science: Usually 3D physical space \((x, y, z)\) + time.
In Data Science / ML: Every measured variable is an axis (\(d\)). Fifty measured variables place each river site in a 50-dimensional space.



The Curse of High Dimensionality (\(n = 100\) sites)


1DTemp


→


3D+ pH, O2


→


50D+ Chemicals & Species


Keeping \(n = 100\) fixed while adding axes makes the space exponentially empty: straight-line Euclidean distances flatten, nearest neighbors stop being similar, and classical models run out of degrees of freedom.







The Methodological Filter

Low \(d\), known mechanism: Exhaust classical statistics first (Correlation, GLMs).
High \(d\), non-linear tabular data: Dimensionality reduction (PCA/UMAP) + Machine Learning (where my PhD fits).
Unstructured data (images/audio/text) or strict logic: Deep Learning or Symbolic AI.






Spoken core: Clarify the word “dimension” first—ecologists think of space and time, whereas ML treats every variable as a new axis. Click 1: walk through the 100 river sites from 1D to 50D; without touching equations, point to the Swiss Roll manifold to show why naive Euclidean distance breaks down when data live on a curved, lower-dimensional structure. Click 2: present the 3-branch filter spanning the whole AI umbrella, and explicitly point out that my PhD sits on Branch #2 (tabular ecotoxicology data needing explainability -> ML).
Callback: Links back to Slide 12’s expertise thought experiment—domain framing comes first, then this filter checks whether AI is justified.
Bridge: Once you land on Machine Learning, how different is it actually from the regressions we already know?

title: AI for Ecotoxicologists
text:
Demystifying ML Under the Hood
Stepping from classical regression into the Machine Learning toolkit on the same environmental dataset:



1. Classical Baseline
Linear trend on a low-dimensional problem: \[Y = ax + b + \varepsilon\]
Solved analytically (e.g., Ordinary Least Squares) under explicit distributional assumptions.




→




2. Same Problem Framed as Machine Learning
Any ML workflow rests on 3 building blocks: (1) Model (equation), (2) Loss Function (error metric: MSE for regression, Cross-Entropy for classification), and (3) Solver (iterative step, e.g., gradient descent).
As non-linearity or dimensionality grows, we step deliberately along the toolkit \(\rightarrow\) Trees, Random Forests, SVMs, or Neural Nets.






Classical Statistics Dictionary


Machine Learning Dictionary




Covariates / Explanatory variables (X)


Features / Inputs




Response variable (Y) & Residuals


Target / Label & Loss Function




Mechanistic / Biological parameters


Weights / Hyperparameters




Key difference: ML weights optimize prediction and rarely carry direct biological meaning. Exhaust classical exploratory data analysis before scaling up.



Spoken core: Demystify ML—it is not magic, just structured optimization (Model + Loss + Solver). Walk through the two-column translation dictionary so people coming from R/biostatistics see the exact parallel terms, then click to stress the red bar: unlike mechanistic parameters, ML weights usually have no direct biological meaning.
Callback: Connects the toolkit hierarchy from Slide 10 to the methodological filter on Slide 15.
Bridge: Now let’s turn this lens onto your own research for two minutes.

Bridge: That third choice—mechanistic inference versus predictive accuracy—takes us straight into Section 3.

title: AI for Ecotoxicologists
text:
Take-Home Messages




AI is an Umbrella Toolkit: Map the taxonomy before choosing an algorithm—GenAI chatbots are only one narrow subset.


Protect Cognitive Friction & Proportionality: Preserve your scientific savoir-faire and weigh the ecological footprint of heavy AI workflows.


Earn Model Complexity: Check true dimensionality and exhaust classical statistical analyses before adopting ML.


Align the Trade-Off to Your Goal: Use domain knowledge to decide where interpretability is essential, where predictive power wins, or where hybrid pipelines bridge both.

title: Let’s Talk About AI
section: Why Learn AI? A Bio-Inspired Paradox
text:
Why Learn AI? A Bio-Inspired Paradox
As a scientist trained to look for mechanistic explanations, why invest in learning “black-box” algorithms?



Biological Signal Integration (Human Learning)

Biological neurons integrate electrochemical inputs across complex networks.
Scientific understanding emerges through effortful cognitive friction—writing, debugging, synthesizing, and testing hypotheses.


[IMAGE: Biological Neuron / Synaptic Integration] Save file as: assets/images/bio_neuron.png 





Artificial Neuron (Perceptron, 1957)

Loosely inspired by biology: Inputs \(\rightarrow\) Weights \(\rightarrow\) Weighted Sum \(\rightarrow\) Activation \(\rightarrow\) Output.
Parameter estimation is numerical loss minimization—not biological reasoning or comprehension.


[IMAGE: Perceptron Diagram (CESAB Day 1 Slide 70)] Save file as: assets/images/artificial_perceptron.png 





The Paradox: AI delivers major scientific breakthroughs (e.g., AlphaFold), yet our most frequent daily contact is with Generative AI chatbots. When misused to bypass writing, literature synthesis, or coding, a bio-inspired tool short-circuits our own biological learning process.

title: Let’s Talk About AI
text:
Epistemic & Ecological Guardrails (Insight 1a)




Cognitive Proletarianization: Externalizing analytical tasks erodes our savoir-faire and methodological metacognition (Stiegler, 2010).
Empirical Evidence on Cognition: Controlled studies indicate that over-reliance on GenAI can reduce knowledge retention (Barcaui, 2025), lower persistence and independent performance (Liu et al., 2026, preprint), and foster dependence/deskilling (Kim et al., 2025).
Illusions of Understanding: Fluent outputs can mask weak epistemic grounding (Messeri & Crockett, 2024)—sparking active debate across French doctoral schools on protecting core research training.
Pragmatic Guardrail: Retain cognitive friction for reasoning, writing, and analysis. Delegate routine formatting or syntax checks; shift from “Do X” to “Critique / explain X”.





Material & Ecological Footprint

Global energy-economy modeling shows AI productivity gains can drive net \(\text{CO}_2\) increases via rebound effects (Alpine et al., 2026).
Infrastructure expansion concentrates in water-stressed regions (e.g., Uruguay: 1.77 and Chile: 3.49 data centers per 1M inhabitants; IFC, 2026).


[IMAGE: IFC 2026 Data Centers Map — Uruguay 1.77] Save file as: assets/images/datacenters_uruguay_ifc2026.png 


“Only a tiny proportion of water in Uruguay is used for human consumption.” — Daniel Pena (Rest of World, 2026)

Navigating the AI Vocabulary
In practice, researchers encounter a scattered soup of overlapping terms and tools:


Linear & Logistic Regression ChatGPT / Claude / Perplexity Symbolic Logic & Rules PCA / UMAP CNN & RNN Data Science & Statistics Random Forest & Decision Trees Intelligent Robots Neural Networks (MLP) Support Vector Machines (SVM) Knowledge Representation


Which field contains which—and where do everyday chatbots actually sit?

title: Let’s Talk About AI
text:
Navigating the AI Vocabulary
Organizing the umbrella into parallel domains and nested subsets:

ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE (Umbrella Discipline)



Symbolic AI, Reasoning & Embodied Systems

Symbolic Logic & Rules Knowledge Representation Intelligent Robots


Explicit rules, ontologies, and constraint solving (e.g., protected-area design in CESAB Day 5).


Overlapping Quantitative Pillar Data Science & Statistics





MACHINE LEARNING (Automated Learning from Data)

Linear & Logistic Regression PCA / UMAP Support Vector Machines (SVM) Random Forest & Decision Trees


DEEP LEARNING (Multi-Layer Neural Networks)

Neural Networks (MLP) CNN & RNN


GENERATIVE AI & LLMs (A small, highly visible subset) ChatGPT / Claude / Perplexity







Standard reference taxonomy: The OECD Framework for the Classification of AI Systems classifies systems by model type (symbolic, statistical, or hybrid), learning paradigm, and transparency.

title: Let’s Talk About AI
section: When Does a Research Problem Need ML?
text:
When Does a Research Problem Need ML?
Scenario: An environmental scientist monitors 100 river sites across chemical concentrations, water quality, climate, and community traits.



What Is a “Dimension”?

In Ecology / Env. Science: Usually 3D physical space \((x, y, z)\) + time.
In Machine Learning: Every measured variable is an axis (\(d\)). Measuring 50 water chemistry & species variables places each site in a 50-dimensional space.



The Curse of High Dimensionality
In a unit hypercube with \(n=100\) samples, the edge length \(l = (k/n)^{1/d}\) needed to capture even \(k=1\) neighbor grows rapidly:



Dimensions (\(d\))
2
3
10
100




Cube edge (\(l\))
0.10
0.21
0.63
0.955



Distance flattens; almost every observation lies near the “border.”




[IMAGE: CESAB Day 1 — Hypercube Distance & 3D-to-2D Manifold] Save file as: assets/images/curse_dim_cube_manifold.png 


The Methodological Filter

Low \(d\), linear/known structure? Traditional statistics are sufficient and preferable.
High \(d\), sparse space? Dimensionality reduction (PCA, UMAP) and ML help uncover lower intrinsic dimensionality (manifolds).

section: Demystifying ML: Scaling One Research Question
text:
Demystifying ML: Scaling One Research Question
Following the same environmental dataset from classical statistics into the ML toolkit:



1. Classical Baseline One predictor, linear trend: \(Y = ax + b + \varepsilon\)
Solved analytically via Ordinary Least Squares.




→




2. Same Problem as ML Any ML workflow = 3 parts:

Model (equation)
Loss function (error metric, e.g., MSE)
Solver (iterative step, e.g., gradient descent)





→




3. Earned Complexity Add non-linear thresholds, categories, or high-\(d\) features:
Move deliberately along the toolkit \(\rightarrow\) Classification (Cross-Entropy), Random Forests, SVMs, or Neural Nets.








Classical Statistics Dictionary


Machine Learning Dictionary


Scientific Note




Covariates / Explanatory variables (\(X\))


Features / Inputs


Domain knowledge guides selection




Response variable (\(Y\)) & Residuals


Target / Label & Loss Function


Defines what is optimized




Mechanistic / Biological parameters


Weights / Hyperparameters


Often have no biological meaning






Check before scaling up: Exhaust classical exploratory data analysis first. Complex algorithms are justified only when data shape and dimensionality demand them.

title: Let’s Talk About AI
section: The Two Cultures & The Flexible Trade-Off
text:
The Two Cultures & The Flexible Trade-Off



Data Modeling Culture (Classical Statistics)

Assumes data arise from a specified stochastic/mechanistic process (e.g., GLMMs, ODEs).
Primary goal: Parameter inference, uncertainty quantification, and causal interpretation.





↔︎




Algorithmic Modeling Culture (Machine Learning)

Treats the underlying data-generating mechanism as unknown or too complex to write analytically.
Primary goal: Out-of-sample predictive accuracy across high-dimensional, non-linear interactions.





High InterpretabilityLinear / Mechanistic (GUTS) ← Hybrid & Explainable AI (XAI) →Decision Trees · Random Forests + Feature Importance High Predictive CapacityDeep Neural Networks


A Pragmatic, Objective-Driven Choice: Interpretability is not a dogma—it is an explicit scientific decision. High-throughput screening (e.g., QSARs) may justify prioritizing accuracy; regulatory or mechanistic risk assessment demands explainability. Increasingly, hybrid pipelines combine both.


Breiman, L. (2001). Statistical modeling: The two cultures. Statistical Science, 16(3), 199–231. 10.1214/ss/1009213726 · Rudin, C. (2019). Stop explaining black box machine learning models for high stakes decisions and use interpretable models instead. Nature Machine Intelligence, 1, 206–215. 10.1038/s42256-019-0048-x

AI is not synonymous with chatbots—it is an organized toolkit spanning symbolic logic, classical ML, deep learning, and generative models.

How These 4 Insights Reshaped My PhD (Preview of Part 2 — Today at 10:45)

Exhausted traditional statistics first (descriptive & linear multivariate audits) before invoking ML.
Kept mechanistic models (GUTS) at the core where biological interpretability is essential.
Deployed ML as an explainable meta-model to audit which experimental design features govern parameter precision.

title: Let’s Talk About AI
text:
Take-Home Messages




AI is an Umbrella Toolkit: Know the taxonomy before choosing an algorithm—GenAI chatbots are only one narrow subset.


Protect Cognitive Friction: Preserve your scientific savoir-faire and remain aware of the ecological footprint of GenAI workflows.


Earn Model Complexity: Check true dimensionality and exhaust classical statistical analyses before adopting ML.


Align the Trade-Off to Your Goal: Use domain knowledge to decide where interpretability is essential, where predictive power wins, or where hybrid approaches bridge both.
